accuracy.evidence: Form and use checked against the National Curriculum in England English Appendix 2 (Year 3: the present perfect form of verbs in contrast to the past tense, He has gone out to play contrasted with He went out to play), the KS2 GPS test framework glossary (present perfect: has or have plus past participle; links past to present), CCSS L.5.1b, the Cambridge Grammar of English and Swan's Practical English Usage entries on present perfect versus simple past, finished-time adverbials (yesterday, ago, last week, in 2019 are not used with the present perfect in standard English) and been versus gone. Irregular participles (eaten, gone, seen, written) verified. The adult text notes American English uses of the simple past with already and yet so the rule is not overstated.

misconceptions.evidence: Targets the documented errors from Swan's Practical English Usage and KS2 GPS mark-scheme distractors: simple past form after has or have (step 1 prediction and wrong-verb feedback, FIX line 2, challenge 'past', m6), she have for she has (build helper feedback, FIX line 1, challenge 'have', m5), finished-time words with the present perfect (step 3 prediction and jar feedback, FIX line 3, challenge 'fin', m2), Has you (FIX line 4, challenge 'has', m8), present simple mistaken for present perfect (challenge 'pres', p5), and gone versus been (step 4, challenge 'gone', p4, m3).

lab_distinct.evidence: flagpperf is about the present perfect's own mechanism: a three-box builder that refuses a helper that does not agree or a simple past form after has or have, two drawn timelines (a boxed finished point versus an arrow reaching NOW) that sentences are dragged onto, a time-word sort into saw and have seen boxes, a home-or-away scene for has gone versus has been, and a wrong-word hunt. flagtense places simple past and progressive sentences on a yesterday-to-now line and spells -ed endings, flagsva is subject-verb agreement; neither builds has or have plus a participle. Gate similarity under 30% to every lab.

lab_teaches.evidence: Learners find each rule by acting: ate is refused after have with the participle named, has is refused for They, a finished-time sentence will not go on the linked-to-now timeline and the reason names the time clue (at 12, in 2019, last week), yesterday is refused from the have seen box, and tapping At home for Dad has gone to the park is refused because he is not back. Completion messages state the rule just discovered.

predictions.evidence: Three predictions with a tempting wrong option that the lab then disproves: 'ate' for I have ___ my lunch (the builder refuses it), 'No, that time is over' for We have lived here since 2019 (the sentence only fits the linked-to-now timeline), and 'Yes, that is fine' for I have seen it yesterday (the jar sort refuses yesterday with have seen).

challenge_feedback.evidence: Six rotating challenge questions with eight distinct wrong-answer messages from why(): simple past after has, she have, a finished-time word with the present perfect, has gone read as back home, a finished-time sentence chosen as still true, the present simple chosen as present perfect, has you, and did with a participle. Every wrong move inside the lab steps also gets its own reason.

readability.evidence: Kid explanation measures 0.1 on learn/readability.py fk_grade (family limit 5.0) and adult 8.6 (limit 10.0). Kid sentences are short and concrete (Dad has gone to the park. He is still there.). Canvas labels are short: 'Sentence 1 of 4: tap has or have, then the verb', 'Finished past time', 'Past linked to now', 'where is Dad now? Tap the place'. The adult text names present perfect, simple past, auxiliary, past participle and time adverbial.

no_filler.evidence: Filler gate clean. Each kid paragraph carries one idea: the two-part form, has versus have and the participle, finished time versus linked to now with time words, and gone versus been. Items spread across form (p1, m1, m5, m6, m8), counting parts (p2), time words (p3, m2, m7), gone and been (p4, m3), meaning now (p5, m4, m9) with no repeated stems.

mobile.evidence: Checked 360 x 640 Android screenshots in light and dark at the start, during Show me and at the end of each step: the three build boxes and four tiles fit, both timelines sit side by side with readable headings and the NOW marker inside the panel, the eight time words sit in two columns, the jar headings were changed to two lines (saw / simple past, have seen / present perfect) after the one-line heading clipped at 360 px, the finished jars grow to show all eight words, the house and park fit side by side, and the slip line scales to fit one row.

accessibility.evidence: Every canvas action has a button twin: the four build tiles, Finished past time and Past linked to now, each time word then the two tense boxes, At home and the destination, and one button per word in the slip line labelled 'Is have wrong?'. The canvas aria-label is rewritten after each action with the result and its reason. walk.cjs runs every task with Show me plus axe WCAG 2.1 AA in light and dark on desktop and iPhone 13 with no console or page errors.
